articles.title: What Is the Moon Base?
articles.summary: This article is for students. NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost. It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore. ______________________________________________________________________ Words to Know outpost: a station or base located in […]
articles.content:
This article is for students.

NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost. It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore.

Artist’s concept depicting astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems, and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at the Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. NASA

______________________________________________________________________

Words to Know

outpost: a station or base located in a remote, distant place

infrastructure: the basic framework and systems that make up a larger building or organization

terrain: the physical features, shape, and layout of the surface of a piece of land, including its slope and elevation

regolith: the layer of loose, fragmented rock and mineral dust covering most of the lunar surface

______________________________________________________________________

Where Will the Moon Base Be Built?

The Moon Base will be built in the lunar South Pole region. This area was selected for its unique lighting conditions and potential for scientific discovery.

Near the lunar South Pole, the Sun stays low on the horizon. Some areas can receive extended periods of sunlight. Other areas stay in shadows for long periods of time. In some craters, sunlight may never reach the surface at all.

Areas that receive extended sunlight could be good for generating solar power. Longer sunlight hours are also good for navigating and exploring. Areas that remain in shadows are some of the coldest areas on the Moon. In these locations, scientists hope to find deposits of frozen water ice.

When Will the Moon Base Be Constructed?

The Moon Base will be constructed in three phases. Each phase will build on what is learned along the way.

Phase One is taking place right now. Over the next few years, NASA and its partners will send robotic missions to explore the lunar South Pole region. They will test new technologies and practice landing on the Moon. This phase will include multiple different landers and lunar terrain vehicles. These missions will conduct science experiments and look for the best locations for building the Moon Base.

Phase Two is planned for 2029-2032. During this period, NASA will begin setting up long-term infrastructure. This includes things like power systems, cargo transportation, and communications hardware. These components will be set up across multiple locations. This will allow for future expansion of the Moon Base.

During Phase Three, NASA will begin assembling a permanent lunar outpost. This is where astronauts will be able to live and work for extended periods. Habitats, power and communication systems, and transportation will all come together to grow Moon Base.

An artist’s concept design of a lunar terrain vehicle. NASA

What Are the Different Components of the Moon Base?

Crewed and robotic lunar rovers will play an important role in the development of the Moon Base. These rovers will test out technologies, transport astronauts, map terrain, and more. Let’s learn about a few of the rovers being built as part of the Moon Base.

NASA’s VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) is fully built. It is being tested at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In 2027, it will launch to the Moon from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its mission will be to explore permanently shadowed craters to look for water and other resources. It will travel more than 15 miles, collecting data and analyzing the lunar soil.

NASA’s PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) is a nuclear-powered rover. It is being built from existing hardware that was created for NASA’s Mars rover missions. PROMISE will look for resources – like potential water ice – on and below the lunar surface. It will carry multiple science instruments, including several that are also on VIPER. The mission is targeted to launch by late 2028.

Lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs) will launch to the lunar South Pole region by 2028. These crewed vehicles will be driven by astronauts during missions to the Moon. This will allow the crew to explore larger areas and gather geology samples. When astronauts are not on the Moon, the LTVs will be remotely operated from Earth. They will map the lunar surface and collect data about the extreme environment in the region.

In addition to rovers, NASA’s MoonFall mission will send a group of propulsive drones to the Moon. They will land near the lunar South Pole by 2028. The drones will descend to the lunar surface independently. They will operate separately over the course of a single lunar day (about 14 Earth days). They will use high-definition cameras to map hard-to-reach terrain. This data will help NASA select potential Artemis landing sites.

What Are the Challenges of Building on the Moon?

The lunar South Pole region is an extreme environment. The Moon doesn’t have any noticeable atmosphere. This means temperatures can reach more than 130°F (54°C) in sunlit areas. And it can be as cold as -334°F (-203°C) inside permanently shadowed craters. This can be very dangerous for astronauts. But it is also a challenge for designing infrastructure and hardware.

Navigating the uneven lunar surface can be difficult. The South Pole region of the Moon has steep slopes, ridges, rocks, and deep craters. Shackleton Crater is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon. Detailed mapping and robotic exploration will help NASA identify safe landing areas and plan routes for astronauts and rovers.

The lunar surface is covered with regolith. This layer of rocky material is the result of meteoroid impacts. Since there is no wind or rain to cause erosion on the lunar surface, regolith particles have sharp edges. This means regolith can quickly wear down spacesuits and equipment. It can be particularly irritating to skin and dangerous if inhaled. Precautions must be taken to keep regolith and lunar dust out of areas where astronauts live.

How Will the Moon Base Prepare Us for Future Missions?

The Moon Base is an important step in learning how to live and work on another world. What we learn on the lunar surface by testing new landing techniques, construction methods, and exploration technologies will help prepare for human missions to Mars.

Exploration geologist Angela Garcia wears a spacesuit prototype while testing science operation techniques for future Artemis missions to the lunar surface. NASA

Career Corner

Here are a few examples of the careers that are making NASA’s Moon Base plans possible:

Space tire engineer: The rovers being designed as part of the Moon Base need to have special tires. Engineers must consider the lack of atmosphere, extreme temperature, and rocky terrain when designing tires to drive long distances on the Moon. A career in engineering demands a strong understanding of math and complex problem-solving. An advanced college degree is usually required. Click here to see a space tire engineer in action.

Exploration geologist: These scientists study rocks and minerals on Earth and throughout the solar system. They look at geological processes to see how erosion and harsh environments can change terrain. For Moon Base, they’re helping to select locations to explore on the lunar surface. And they’re helping train the astronauts who will land and gather samples. This career requires strong observational skills and usually requires an advanced college degree. Click here to see what it’s like being an exploration geologist at NASA.

Manufacturing technician: Turning designs into reality takes skilled technicians. Fabrication and assembly of robotic equipment and spacecraft parts requires precise calculations. Being able to follow intricate instructions is key. Trade school training and skills such as operating forklifts and heavy machinery may be required.

Instrument technician: These experts install, calibrate, and maintain sensors and control systems. They troubleshoot issues that might come up with delicate systems and equipment. This career path often starts with an apprenticeship or hands-on training alongside experienced technicians. An associate’s degree is often required. Click here to see some of the testing completed on one of the Moon Base landers.

articles.personality_title: NASA plans first Moon Base at lunar South Pole with phased robotic and crewed missions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA is preparing to send astronauts back to the Moon, aiming to stay longer this time. They plan to build the first permanent Moon Base where astronauts can live and work while exploring the lunar surface.

**What happened** – The Moon Base will be built in the lunar South Pole region, chosen for its unique sunlight and shadow conditions. Construction will happen in three phases: first, robotic missions now through the mid-2020s will explore and test technologies; second, from 2029 to 2032, NASA will install infrastructure like power and communication systems; third, astronauts will begin living and working at the base with habitats and vehicles. Several rovers, including VIPER and PROMISE, will explore the area to find resources like water ice.

**Impact** – This project is important because it will help scientists understand how to live and work on another world for long periods. The Moon’s extreme temperatures, rough terrain, and dusty surface present big challenges, so testing technology and mapping the area is crucial. Finding frozen water could support future missions by providing drinking water and rocket fuel.

**What's next step** – Robotic missions will continue exploring the South Pole to gather data and test equipment. By 2027 and 2028, rovers like VIPER and PROMISE will launch to search for water and map the terrain. After setting up infrastructure in the early 2030s, astronauts will begin building and living at the Moon Base.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s phased plan to build a Moon Base at the lunar South Pole combines robotic exploration and astronaut missions to prepare for sustained human presence beyond Earth.
articles.personality_title_fr: La NASA prévoit la première base lunaire au pôle Sud avec des missions robotiques et habitées en plusieurs étapes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La NASA se prépare à renvoyer des astronautes sur la Lune, avec l’objectif d’y rester plus longtemps. Elle prévoit de construire la première base lunaire permanente où les astronautes pourront vivre, travailler et explorer la surface lunaire.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La base lunaire sera construite dans la région du pôle Sud lunaire, choisie pour ses conditions uniques d’ensoleillement et d’ombre. La construction se fera en trois phases : d’abord, des missions robotiques entre maintenant et le milieu des années 2020 exploreront et testeront des technologies ; ensuite, de 2029 à 2032, la NASA installera des infrastructures comme des systèmes d’énergie et de communication ; enfin, les astronautes commenceront à vivre et travailler à la base avec des habitats et des véhicules. Plusieurs rovers, comme VIPER et PROMISE, exploreront la région pour chercher des ressources comme de la glace d’eau.

**Impact** – Ce projet est important car il aidera les scientifiques à comprendre comment vivre et travailler longtemps sur un autre monde. Les températures extrêmes, le terrain accidenté et la poussière lunaire posent de gros défis, donc tester les technologies et cartographier la zone est essentiel. Trouver de la glace pourrait soutenir les futures missions en fournissant de l’eau potable et du carburant.

**Prochaine étape** – Les missions robotiques continueront d’explorer le pôle Sud pour collecter des données et tester les équipements. En 2027 et 2028, les rovers VIPER et PROMISE seront lancés pour chercher de l’eau et cartographier le terrain. Après l’installation des infrastructures au début des années 2030, les astronautes commenceront à construire et habiter la base lunaire.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Le plan en plusieurs étapes de la NASA pour construire une base lunaire au pôle Sud combine exploration robotique et missions habitées pour préparer une présence humaine durable au-delà de la Terre.
articles.personality_title_es: La NASA planea la primera base lunar en el polo sur con misiones robóticas y tripuladas por fases
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La NASA se está preparando para enviar astronautas de regreso a la Luna, con la intención de que permanezcan más tiempo. Planean construir la primera base lunar permanente donde los astronautas puedan vivir, trabajar y explorar la superficie lunar.

**Qué pasó** – La base lunar se construirá en la región del polo sur lunar, elegida por sus condiciones únicas de luz solar y sombra. La construcción tendrá tres fases: primero, misiones robóticas desde ahora hasta mediados de la década de 2020 explorarán y probarán tecnologías; segundo, entre 2029 y 2032, la NASA instalará infraestructura como sistemas de energía y comunicación; tercero, los astronautas comenzarán a vivir y trabajar en la base con hábitats y vehículos. Varias rovers, incluidos VIPER y PROMISE, explorarán el área para encontrar recursos como hielo de agua.

**Impacto** – Este proyecto es importante porque ayudará a los científicos a aprender cómo vivir y trabajar por largos períodos en otro mundo. Las temperaturas extremas, el terreno accidentado y el polvo lunar presentan grandes desafíos, por lo que es vital probar tecnologías y mapear la zona. articles.title: Thank You for Doing NASA Science!
articles.summary: It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, […]
articles.content:
It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, we’re deeply grateful for your help.

Here are a few more messages of gratitude our scientists sent in to share with you.

Chihoko Cullens, principal investigator (PI) of the Space Cloud Watch project, said: “Thank you to Pirjo Koski, Huub Eggen, and Brian Scott! Pirjo posts beautiful Noctilucent Cloud photos and has introduced us to other cloud databases in the Netherlands. Huub goes beyond basic data requested by us and actively discusses his observations providing helpful insights. Brian contributes consistently and has provided us with useful time-lapse videos. All three volunteers have consistently provided much needed data and have contributed their time in developing our Field Guide that now helps new citizen scientists correctly identify and report their observations. We are grateful for their contributions.”

Ryan Scott from the Open Science Data Repository Analysis Working Groups (OSDR AWGs) project said: “A cohort of high school students took NASA’s free Machine Learning for Space Biology course and then kept working as citizen science volunteers. Guided by OSDR AWG members​ who also gave their time freely, they mined open-access retinal data from the International Space Station (ISS) Rodent Research-9 Mission in the NASA Open Science Data Repository and trained a machine learning ensemble that separates oxidative damage from cell death in the eyes of space-flown mice, now published in the scientific journal npj Microgravity: Machine learning ensemble reveals distinct molecular pathways of retinal damage in spaceflown mice. Every citizen science student co-author earned authorship, and many of those listed above started college this fall with a NASA publication already behind them. Thanks to Aditi Adapala, Mushtaq Ali, Naomi Z. Chang, Sophie Cai, Margaret Hitt, Anishka Jain, Matthew Lin, MarcAnthony Paolieri Della Monica, Elior Paley, Rudransh Pathak, Shawnak Samaddar, Shriya Sawant, Zhihan Shi, Rohin Sood, Fabian P. Uribe, Maxwell Volkan, and Jessica Wu, plus OSDR AWG members Anna Lewkowicz, Sunny Narayanan, Daniya Thomas, Ethan Waisberg, Pinar Avci, Joshua Ong, Marshall Tabetah, Richard Barker, Lauren Sanders, and Xiao Wen ‘Vivien’ Mao.”

Kyra Shaw, project coordinator for Snapshot Wisconsin at the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, said: “Our team has a Thanksgiving thank-you message for Snapshot volunteer Tim Sparks. Tim has been a dedicated Snapshot Wisconsin volunteer for nearly 10 years. Tim went above and beyond these past two years by helping to pilot test protocols and then joining the full launch for a new initiative, the Snapshot Phenology Project. Joining a select group of volunteers, Tim set up and is maintaining extra equipment to measure snow depth, temperature, and sound recordings at his Snapshot trail camera site. Thank you, Tim, for joining in our events, sending in your favorite photos, and going the extra mile to make the Snapshot Phenology Project a success!”

Benjamin Fernando from the Impact Flash! project said: "Thank you to everyone who’s been sending in images of the Moon! A special thanks to Joerg Tomczak, who helped us with the Artemis II campaign!”

Rachael Mady from the Chesapeake Water Watch project said: “We are so thankful for all of our volunteers! Since 2021, volunteers have been with us every step of the way and have made Chesapeake Water Watch possible. The Chesapeake Bay is the nation's largest estuary, and we had people all over submitting observations and helping us cross our 6,000 observation milestone this year. While the project may be wrapping up, the impact that our volunteers have on improving the health of the Bay will continue for years to come. Thanks for all that you do!”

Marc Kuchner, from the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 science team, said: “Thank you to Prateek Singh for creating new tools for astronomy and for helping us lead our Space Apps challenge! Thank you to Bruce Baller and Katharina Doll for sharing their lists of brown dwarf discoveries and for inspiring all of us! Thank you to Frank Kiwy for his latest batch of python tools – shared with everyone – that dig through Pan-STARRS, WISE, SIMBAD, Gaia DR3, CatWISE, and NSC DR2 data! Thank you to Michiharu Hyogo for keeping the new publications coming, Hugo Durantini Luca, Jim Rabe, and Lisa Stiller for helping keep us all connected, Peter Jalowiczor for traveling around the world in the snow, and to Farid Cedeno and Martin Bilsing for teaching others about our project!”

Emma Yates, PI of the Ozone Where We Live (OWWL) project, said: “We have developed an amazing collaboration with Quest Science Center, a non-profit that among many other things supports high school students interested in the Earth’s climate. One of the aspects of Quest is to develop student-run studies by pairing high school students with mentors. OWWL has been working with these students and their Quest mentors to study air quality in the Tri-Valley Region in California (Bay Area into San Joaquin Valley). We designed a mini field campaign over the month of August, with 12 science flights and ground-based sensors at participants' homes. I know the students (and mentors) would get a kick out of seeing their work highlighted by NASA!”

Everyone can join the fun and make a lasting mark on NASA science. You’ll find all our open opportunities at https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/. Happy Thanksgiving!

articles.personality_title: NASA thanks volunteers for helping make important science discoveries
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every year, NASA works with volunteers from all over the world to help with important science projects. These volunteers collect and analyze data, write computer programs, and even create their own experiments. This teamwork helps NASA learn more about space, the Earth, and the environment.

**What happened** – During Thanksgiving, NASA expressed gratitude to its many citizen scientists. Volunteers contributed to projects like observing clouds, studying space biology with machine learning, monitoring wildlife in Wisconsin, tracking moon impacts, and measuring air quality in California. For example, high school students helped analyze eye damage in mice that have been to space and even earned co-authorship on a published scientific paper. Other volunteers have spent years collecting data that supports environmental research.

**Impact** – These volunteer efforts have led to real scientific discoveries and improved understanding in fields like astronomy, biology, and environmental science. The work has helped NASA publish new research, improve data collection methods, and involve people of all ages in science. This broad participation shows how everyday people can contribute to big science projects and make a difference.

**What's next step** – NASA encourages more people to join its citizen science projects through its website. New volunteers can participate by collecting data, analyzing information, or helping develop new tools. This ongoing collaboration will continue to support NASA’s mission and inspire future discoveries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s citizen scientists play a vital role in advancing space and Earth science by contributing data, analysis, and ideas that lead to meaningful discoveries.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque année, la NASA collabore avec des bénévoles du monde entier pour l’aider dans des projets scientifiques importants. Ces bénévoles collectent et analysent des données, écrivent des programmes informatiques et créent même leurs propres expériences. Ce travail d’équipe aide la NASA à mieux comprendre l’espace, la Terre et l’environnement.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Pendant la période de Thanksgiving, la NASA a exprimé sa gratitude envers ses nombreux citoyens scientifiques. Les bénévoles ont contribué à des projets comme l’observation des nuages, l’étude de la biologie spatiale avec l’apprentissage automatique, la surveillance de la faune dans le Wisconsin, le suivi des impacts lunaires et la mesure de la qualité de l’air en Californie. D’autres bénévoles consacrent des années à collecter des données qui soutiennent la recherche environnementale.

Cette large participation montre comment chacun peut contribuer à de grands projets scientifiques et faire une différence.

**Prochaine étape** – La NASA encourage davantage de personnes à rejoindre ses projets de science citoyenne via son site internet. Les nouveaux bénévoles peuvent participer en collectant des données, en analysant des informations ou en aidant à développer de nouveaux outils. **Résumé en une phrase** – Les citoyens scientifiques de la NASA jouent un rôle essentiel dans l’avancement des sciences spatiales et terrestres en apportant des données, des analyses et des idées qui mènent à des découvertes importantes.
articles.personality_title_es: La NASA agradece a los voluntarios por ayudar a lograr importantes descubrimientos científicos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada año, la NASA trabaja con voluntarios de todo el mundo para ayudar en importantes proyectos científicos. Estos voluntarios recolectan y analizan datos, escriben programas de computadora e incluso crean sus propios experimentos. Este trabajo en equipo ayuda a la NASA a aprender más sobre el espacio, la Tierra y el medio ambiente.

**Qué pasó** – Durante el Día de Acción de Gracias, la NASA expresó su gratitud a sus muchos científicos ciudadanos. Los voluntarios contribuyeron a proyectos como la observación de nubes, el estudio de biología espacial con aprendizaje automático, el monitoreo de la vida silvestre en Wisconsin, el seguimiento de impactos en la Luna y la medición de la calidad del aire en California. Por ejemplo, estudiantes de secundaria ayudaron a analizar daños en los ojos de ratones que viajaron al espacio y hasta fueron coautores de un artículo científico publicado. Otros voluntarios han dedicado años a recolectar datos que apoyan la investigación ambiental.

**Impacto** – Estos esfuerzos voluntarios han llevado a descubrimientos científicos reales y a una mejor comprensión en áreas como la astronomía, la biología y la ciencia ambiental. El trabajo ha ayudado a la NASA a publicar nuevas investigaciones, mejorar métodos de recolección de datos e involucrar a personas de todas las edades en la ciencia. Esta amplia participación muestra cómo cualquier persona puede contribuir a grandes proyectos científicos y marcar la diferencia.

**Próximo paso** – La NASA anima a más personas a unirse a sus proyectos de ciencia ciudadana a través de su sitio web. Los nuevos voluntarios pueden participar recolectando datos, analizando información o ayudando a desarrollar nuevas herramientas. Esta colaboración continuará apoyando la misión de la NASA e inspirando futuros descubrimientos.

**Una frase clave** – Los científicos ciudadanos de la NASA juegan un papel vital en el avance de la ciencia espacial y terrestre al aportar datos, análisis e ideas que conducen a descubrimientos importantes.

articles.title: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger
articles.summary: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb […]
articles.content:
Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

“Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.”

Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy

In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler

Before their transformation, the two stars spent millennia placidly orbiting one another as a binary pair. But once the smaller star came into contact with the surface of the giant star, their “unification” happened after only seven orbits (about seven years). Other known binary star mergers, featuring two smaller stars, occurred after thousands of orbits.

“We thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,” said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. “One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!”

“When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect — a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao’s data,” said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. “As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star’s outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.”

This is the beginning of a high-stakes showdown some binary stars go through, known as a common envelope evolution. The gas between the stars at this stage is known as a common envelope because its outer layer is shared between them. In this system, the primary star engulfed the smaller star and the companion plummeted, spiraling through the envelope as it was robbed of orbital energy by drag. While Webb’s data proved the stars merged, a merger wasn’t the only possible outcome for this system.

In other systems, both stars survive the process — shedding a lot of mass along the way, but remaining independent in tight orbits. Over time, such surviving pairs can transform into neutron stars and black holes, explode as supernovae, produce ripples in space-time known as gravitational waves, and create millisecond pulsars.

Hitting “replay”

The team reconstructed what happened to Bao by updating their ongoing simulations. They found the model that matched Webb’s mid-infrared observations, which detailed the dust shed by the more massive primary star over centuries.

The team concluded that prior to the eruption, Bao’s primary star dwarfed the Sun: It was seven times as massive, 350 times the radius, and 18,000 times brighter — making “Big Bao” an appropriate nickname.

“It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,” said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Their modeling resulted in the first mass estimate for the smaller, now demolished, companion. Compared to our Sun, they found that “Little Bao” was likely less massive (about 0.7 solar masses), with a slightly smaller radius and fainter.

After revealing the masses of the pair, the model showed there might be leftover energy for Little Bao to “flee” the scene. However, further analysis determined that Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao's core. Their encounter was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,” De said.

What does the new star — now simply Bao — look like today? Only future observations will identify how its “heft” settles.

Image: Andromeda Star Merger (Artist's Concept)

Top to bottom, left to right: In this artist’s concept, the stars are surrounded by a dust shell pre-merger; the stars brightened and the companion star’s orbit began to slow as the larger star engulfed it; the eruption occurred; dust freely expands at the poles after the merger. Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia)

Reconstructing what happened

While Webb’s data allowed the team to measure how much mass was ejected during this process and how efficient the process of common envelope evolution was, Karambelkar’s team also used observations that span ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light from several telescopes to watch the events, often as they unfolded. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.)

Bao first caught the team’s attention in February 2023, when they saw an unusual variable star in data from NASA’s retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission. Before 2018, the object had a consistent luminosity. Observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) in September 2024 showed that Bao was not only beginning to brighten, but also spew dust.

When NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) serendipitously saw Bao fade rapidly in visible light and brighten in infrared light during a routine survey in July 2025, the researchers knew it was an indicator of unusual activity. The Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, watching the stars rapidly brighten and radically heat up.

In November 2025, the team received fast-turn observations from NASA’s now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope in Hawaii. Webb’s observations were taken on Dec. 24, 2025, as part of a just-in-time Director’s Discretionary Time program.

New path for future research

The team’s analysis of Bao, formally known as AT 2025abao, offers an approach to reconstructing the events: They conducted their analysis and made observations of the stars’ merger in real time. That allowed them to measure how efficient common envelope evolution is. In other cases, astronomers have worked to carefully reverse-engineer events that may have happened hundreds or even millions of years ago.

The new finding comes about just as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to conduct vast publicly available surveys. Its Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey will yield a huge number of new transient events that could benefit from similar analyses. “There’s going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead,” Karambelkar said.

This work is funded in part by a grant from NASA’s Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

articles.personality_title: NASA captures first-ever star merger in Andromeda galaxy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Stars often live in pairs called binary systems, orbiting each other for millions of years. Sometimes, these stars merge into one, but such events are rare and hard to watch as they happen.

**What happened** – In 2023, scientists spotted a strange star in the Andromeda galaxy that was slowly getting brighter. By 2025, they saw it erupt. Using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope and other observatories, they confirmed that a smaller star had spiraled into and merged with a giant supergiant star. They named this new star Bao.

**Impact** – This is the first time astronomers have observed a stellar merger like this in real time and studied it so quickly after the event. The smaller star merged after just seven orbits, much faster than other known mergers. This helps scientists understand how stars can combine and how such mergers might create unusual stars or lead to other cosmic events like black holes.

**What's next step** – Researchers will keep watching Bao to see how the new star changes over time. NASA’s upcoming space telescopes, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, will find many more events like this, allowing scientists to learn more about how stars live and die.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, NASA has observed and studied a star merging with a giant companion in another galaxy, opening new doors to understanding stellar evolution.

Ils ont nommé cette nouvelle étoile Bao.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois que des astronomes observent une fusion stellaire de ce type en temps réel et l’étudient si rapidement après l’événement. Cela aide les scientifiques à comprendre comment les étoiles peuvent se combiner et comment ces fusions peuvent créer des étoiles inhabituelles ou mener à d’autres phénomènes cosmiques comme les trous noirs.

articles.personality_title_es: La NASA capta por primera vez la fusión de estrellas en la galaxia de Andrómeda
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las estrellas a menudo viven en pares llamados sistemas binarios, girando una alrededor de la otra durante millones de años. A veces, estas estrellas se fusionan en una sola, pero estos eventos son raros y difíciles de observar en tiempo real.

**Qué pasó** – En 2023, los científicos notaron una estrella extraña en la galaxia de Andrómeda que se estaba volviendo más brillante lentamente. Para 2025, vieron una erupción. Usando el telescopio espacial James Webb de la NASA y otros observatorios, confirmaron que una estrella más pequeña se había enroscado y fusionado con una estrella supergigante. Llamaron a esta nueva estrella Bao.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que los astrónomos observan una fusión estelar así en tiempo real y la estudian tan rápido después del evento. La estrella más pequeña se fusionó después de solo siete órbitas, mucho más rápido que otras fusiones conocidas. Esto ayuda a los científicos a entender cómo las estrellas pueden combinarse y cómo estas fusiones pueden crear estrellas inusuales o llevar a otros eventos cósmicos como agujeros negros.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán observando a Bao para ver cómo cambia esta nueva estrella con el tiempo. Los próximos telescopios espaciales de la NASA, como el telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman, encontrarán muchos más eventos similares, permitiendo a los científicos aprender más sobre cómo viven y mueren las estrellas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Por primera vez, la NASA ha observado y estudiado una estrella fusionándose con un gigante en otra galaxia, abriendo nuevas puertas para entender la evolución estelar.

articles.title: Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03273-yLong-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope.
articles.content:
NEWS AND VIEWS

18 November 2026 Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star Long-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope. By Jason Nordhaus 0 Jason Nordhaus Jason Nordhaus is at the Center for Computational Relativity and Gravitation and the National Technical Institute for the Deaf, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York 14623, USA. View author publications PubMed Google Scholar Save article View saved research

Towards the end of their lives, stars experience a drastic change in their structure as they swell and enter what is known as their giant phase. Because most stars are thought to host orbiting companions (such as planets, other stars or black holes), interesting interactions can happen as the giant host expands. The most striking of these occur when a companion star is engulfed by a giant: astronomers refer to this as the common-envelope phase1. Despite theoretical expectations that common envelopes should be widespread in stellar evolution, they have been extraordinarily difficult to observe. Writing in Nature, however, Karambelkar et al.2 report the first direct detection of a star inside a giant star.

Nature 659, 599-600 (2026)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03273-y

articles.personality_title: Astronomers observe a star inside a giant star for the first time
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – When stars get old, they grow very large and become what scientists call giant stars. Many stars have other stars or planets orbiting around them. Sometimes, when a giant star expands, it can swallow a smaller star inside it. This is called the common-envelope phase, but it has never been seen directly before.

**What happened** – A team of astronomers watched a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy over a long time. They discovered, for the first time, that another star was inside the giant star’s outer layers. They saw how the smaller star’s orbit was slowly shrinking as it moved inside the giant star.

**Impact** – This is an important discovery because it confirms a theory about how stars change and interact. Seeing a star inside another star helps scientists understand more about how stars live and die. It also helps explain how some unusual star systems form.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to watch this star system and look for others like it. Studying these rare events will improve models of star behavior and may reveal new details about the life cycles of stars.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, astronomers have directly observed a star orbiting inside a giant star, shedding new light on how stars evolve and interact.
